title: Aftershock productivity: rupture area or seismic moment as the orthopolic resource
status: Specified and committed BEFORE any aftershock count was computed from the catalogue. The git history of this file is the preregistration record. The prediction itself was first committed in docs/resource-catalogue.md (commit e4bf526).
prior_exposure: The frozen catalogue data/raw/usgs_2010_2024.csv was analysed before for Gutenberg-Richter b-values only (b = 0.998 [0.973, 1.024], Mw >= 5.5). No space-time clustering, mainshock selection or aftershock count has been computed.

The registrant knows that published aftershock-productivity exponents are commonly reported between about 0.8 and 1.1. This test is therefore a replication on frozen data under a fixed pipeline, testing a second consequence of the rupture-area reading of Gutenberg-Richter; it is not blind to the literature.
question: Does the expected number of aftershocks of a mainshock scale with its rupture area (the territory reading of earthquake size statistics) or with its seismic moment (the energy reading)?

H_area.why: Aftershock sites are allocated per unit rupture area; self-similar scaling gives A ∝ M0^(2/3) ∝ 10^(1.0 M).

H_moment.why: Aftershocks are allocated per unit seismic moment (energy); M0 ∝ 10^(1.5 M).

H_width.why: Secondary. Width-saturated rupture (Hanks and Bakun 2002, M0 ∝ A^2 above about M 6.7) gives A ∝ 10^(0.75 M). The global set mixes saturated and unsaturated ruptures, so a mixture would fall between 0.75 and 1.

data.events: Rows with time before 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z and magType starting with 'mw' (as in the pilot); magnitudes rounded to 0.1.

declustering.method: Gardner and Knopoff (1974) windows. Distance d(M) = 10^(0.1238 M + 0.983) km (great-circle distance between epicentres); time t(M) = 10^(0.032 M + 2.7389) days for M >= 6.5, else 10^(0.5409 M - 0.547) days.
declustering.procedure: Process events in decreasing magnitude (ties: earlier first). An unassigned event becomes a mainshock; every unassigned smaller-or-equal event within d(M) and within t(M) after it, or within t(M) before it, is assigned to its cluster.
declustering.mainshocks_analysed: Mainshocks with M >= 6.5 whose full time window ends before 2025-01-01.
declustering.aftershock_count: N_i = number of events assigned to mainshock i that occur after it, with M >= 5.5.

estimator.model: Poisson regression of N_i on M_i: E[N_i] = K 10^(alpha (M_i - 6.5)), maximum likelihood.
estimator.uncertainty: Percentile 95% interval from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of mainshocks (seed 20261008), which accommodates overdispersion.
estimator.reported_also: Negative-binomial fit as a check on the point estimate; b-value of the analysed catalogue for comparison with alpha.

decision_rule.support_H_width: Reported if the interval contains 0.75 and excludes 1.0; a mixture is then the likely reading.
decision_rule.primary: Gardner-Knopoff windows, mw-family magnitudes, all depths.

sensitivity: Rupture-length windows: distance max(d(M), L(M)) with Wells and Coppersmith (1994) subsurface length log10 L = -2.44 + 0.59 M km, time 365 days.
Exclude aftershocks in the first day after the mainshock (short-term incompleteness after large events).
limitations: A global M >= 5.5 catalogue counts only the largest aftershocks, so smaller mainshocks mostly have zero or one; the slope is driven by M >= 7 events.
Gardner-Knopoff distance windows are smaller than the ruptures of the largest earthquakes, which can bias alpha downwards; the rupture-length sensitivity addresses this.
No focal mechanisms are available to separate width-saturated strike-slip events.
